div.head: About the eLiebermann Project
div.p: eLiebermann is a digital research platform for the laws and legal language of England before the Norman Conquest. Its foundation is Felix Liebermann's Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen (1903–16), still the standard edition of the early English laws, which it makes searchable, interlinked and readable in English for the first time. Around that core it brings together later editions, translations and scholarship, so that the text of a law, the words it uses, and what scholars have said about both can be studied in one place.
The platform has three parts:

list.item: The eLiebermann Law Codes Database presents the laws clause by clause. Each clause gives the Old English or Latin text as Liebermann prints it, labelled by manuscript; his German translation, with an English rendering of it; and, where they exist, the texts and translations of later editors. Every clause is indexed by the offences, people and places it concerns, and is linked to the other clauses that Liebermann and later scholars compare with it.

The eLiebermann Legal Dictionary is a digital edition of Liebermann's Wörterbuch (volume II, part 1), the dictionary of the Old English, Latin and French words of the laws. Every abbreviation, siglum and grammatical term in an entry is linked to its expansion and translation, every law it cites is linked to that clause in the Law Codes Database, and headwords are linked to the Bosworth–Toller Anglo-Saxon Dictionary.

The eLiebermann Guide to the Gesetze expands and translates the apparatus of the edition: Liebermann's sigla for the law codes, his list of manuscripts, and his grammatical abbreviations, with his own account of how to read the dictionary.

div.p: The project grows out of research on the language and style of the earliest English law codes at the University of Hong Kong. Its aims are to open Liebermann's work to readers who do not read his German; to give the legal vocabulary of the laws a complete and fully referenced lexicon; and to make possible new questions about how the laws were written: how their vocabulary relates to that of other Old English writing, including poetry, and how legislative style developed between the seventh century and the eleventh.
At present eLiebermann holds:

list.item: 9,246 dictionary entries, the whole of the Wörterbuch;
2,547 clauses from 78 law codes and legal texts, from the laws of Æthelberht of Kent to those of William I and Henry I;

the texts and translations of the principal modern editions, among them those of F. L. Attenborough, A. J. Robertson, Dorothy Whitelock, Lisi Oliver, Stefan Jurasinski and Lisi Oliver, Andrew Rabin, and A. G. Kennedy;
1,348 cross-references between clauses from Liebermann's margins, and about 1,500 more from later scholars, each linked in both directions.

div.p: eLiebermann is a work in progress. New material is added, and existing material corrected, continuously; every change is recorded (see Code and data, below).

div.head: Felix Liebermann and Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen
div.p: Felix Liebermann (born Berlin, 20 July 1851; died Berlin, 7 October 1925) was a German historian of medieval England, and the foremost authority of his generation on Anglo-Saxon and Anglo-Norman law. He came from a prosperous Jewish family in Berlin; the painter Max Liebermann was his elder brother. He began in business, in banking and the textile trade, and it was while he was living in Manchester that he became interested in English history. In 1873 he went to Göttingen to study it under Georg Waitz and Reinhold Pauli, and took his doctorate in 1875 with a study of the Dialogus de Scaccario. From 1877 to 1885 he worked as an editor for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica, for which he edited extracts from thirteenth-century English historians.

Liebermann held no regular university post, and spent the rest of his life as an independent scholar in Berlin. In a long series of studies he edited and explained the legal compilations of the early twelfth century through which most of the Old English laws were transmitted: the Quadripartitus (1892), the Consiliatio Cnuti (1893), the Leges Edwardi Confessoris (1896) and the Leges Henrici (1901). The universities of Oxford and Cambridge gave him honorary degrees in 1896. His English lecture The National Assembly in the Anglo-Saxon Period appeared in 1913.
His great work, Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, was published in Halle for the Savigny-Stiftung, in three volumes and four parts:

list.item: I. Text und Übersetzung (1903): the texts of all the laws, from Æthelberht to the Anglo-Norman compilations, with the readings of every manuscript printed in parallel columns, a German translation, and marginal cross-references between clauses;
II.1. Wörterbuch (1906): a dictionary of every word in the laws;
II.2. Rechts- und Sachglossar (1912): a glossary of legal and historical subjects;
III. Einleitung zu jedem Stück; Erklärungen zu einzelnen Stellen (1916): an introduction to each text and a commentary on individual passages.

div.p: More than a century later the Gesetze remains the edition from which the laws are cited, and much of what has been written on early English law since rests on it. But it is not an easy book to use. It is written in a heavily abbreviated academic German, its apparatus depends on hundreds of sigla, and in its printed form it cannot be searched. Parts of its scholarship have also been revised, by Patrick Wormald and others. eLiebermann keeps Liebermann's text as he printed it, and sets beside it the work of the century since.

div.head: How Entries Are Made
div.p: Both the Legal Dictionary and the Law Codes Database are built from the printed Gesetze, and both add material that Liebermann does not have. The editorial workflow combines human scholarship with machine-assisted transcription, collation and encoding. The division of labour is fixed: machine processes produce and compare text; human editors set the editorial rules, resolve every disputed reading against the printed page, and decide what is published.
div.head: Transcription and collation
div.p: Every dictionary entry has been transcribed twice, independently. A machine transcription was made from page images of the Wörterbuch by Claude, a large language model developed by Anthropic; separately, the project team keyed the entries by hand into Word documents. The two transcriptions are then collated entry by entry and word by word. Agreement between two independent transcriptions is strong evidence that a reading is right. Each disagreement is classified (a slip in one transcription or the other, a difference of typography only, a different division between entries) and, where it cannot be settled from the transcriptions alone, it is checked by an editor against the printed volume. A report of every collation, and a running list of readings still to be checked against the print, are published with the project's data.

Typography is transcribed as carefully as the words, because in Liebermann it carries meaning: roman type is the language of the laws, italic is Liebermann's German, bold marks headwords, and a superscript L or F marks a Latin or French word. Page breaks are recorded, so that every entry is linked to its page in a scan of the printed volume.
div.head: Encoding and linking
div.p: Every dictionary entry and every law-code clause is a separate file in TEI XML, the international standard for scholarly digital editions (Text Encoding Initiative, P5). Within an entry, law-code sigla, manuscript sigla and grammatical abbreviations are identified automatically, by longest match against the project's authority lists, and linked to their expansions; law codes are linked only in roman type, so that Liebermann's German is never mistaken for a citation. Each citation of a law is then normalised to a standard key (law code and clause number) and resolved to its clause in the Law Codes Database. Liebermann's own cross-references between entries (s. WORD) become links, and headwords are linked to the Bosworth–Toller Anglo-Saxon Dictionary.
div.head: The Law Codes Database
div.p: The database is compiled in a master spreadsheet of more than fifty fields for each clause, from which the clause files are generated by script. For each clause it records Liebermann's text of each manuscript he prints, identified by his siglum, with his page and section number; his German translation; and an English rendering of his German. That rendering is a deliberately close, semi-literal translation made with Claude, so that readers can follow what Liebermann understood the law to say. It is labelled as such on every clause page, is not a new translation of the Old English, and is being reviewed. The texts and translations of modern editions are entered with their page references and checked against the printed books. Liebermann's 1,348 marginal cross-references were transcribed from the page images of volume I, and those of later scholars collected from their editions, footnotes and tables of sources; each records its source and page, and each is linked in both directions. The subject index of offences, people and places is the project's own editorial work.
Checking is recorded clause by clause: the foot of each clause page says what has been checked, and against which page of which book. At present 2,133 of the 2,547 clauses carry such a record.
div.head: Review and publication
div.p: All the project's text and data are kept under version control in a public Git repository. Every addition or correction, by a person or by a script, is proposed as a separate, documented change, and is published only when an editor has reviewed and approved it. The full history of every file, with the date and reason for each change, can be seen there. Errors can be reported, and new entries suggested, through Make a suggestion or the Suggest a change link at the foot of every entry.

div.head: Citing eLiebermann
div.p: When you cite eLiebermann, please cite the entry or clause you used, with its address and the date you consulted it, and also the printed edition on which it is based:
Felix Liebermann, ed. and trans., Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, 3 vols (Halle: Niemeyer, 1903–16).
Every dictionary entry and every clause page gives the volume and page of the printed edition, so that it can be cited too.

A dictionary entry: “bocland”, eLiebermann Legal Dictionary, ed. Anya Adair, https://notamitchell.github.io/law/entry.html?id=bocland (accessed 15 October 2026); after Felix Liebermann, ed. and trans., Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, 3 vols (Halle: Niemeyer, 1903–16), II.1, p. 26.

A law-code clause: “Ine 23.2”, eLiebermann Law Codes Database, ed. Anya Adair, https://notamitchell.github.io/law/law.html?id=Ine_23-2 (accessed 15 October 2026); after Felix Liebermann, ed. and trans., Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, 3 vols (Halle: Niemeyer, 1903–16), I, p. 98.
When you quote a modern edition or translation from a clause page, please cite that edition as well; its full reference is given on the page.

div.head: People
div.p: Dr Anya Adair, Principal Investigator and General Editor. School of English and Department of Law, The University of Hong Kong. Anya Adair directs the project and is responsible for its editorial policy, the translations, the subject index of the laws, and the final review of all entries.
Dr Mitchell Harrop, Website and Technical Development. Mitchell Harrop designed and built the eLiebermann website and its data infrastructure.
Allan Adair, Research Assistant. Allan Adair transcribes entries and checks them against the printed edition.

div.head: Code and data
div.p: The site's code and all its data are on GitHub at github.com/notamitchell/law: the dictionary entries and clauses as TEI XML, the authority lists of law codes, manuscripts and abbreviations, the scripts that build the site, and the reports of collation and checking.

Liebermann's text and translation are in the public domain. The texts and translations of modern editions shown on clause pages remain the copyright of their authors and publishers, and are not offered for reuse.
